channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Dr. Mark Hyman on Function Health & GLP-1 microdosing | E2334
gist: Function Health co-founder Dr. Mark Hyman describes a $365/year, hundreds-of-thousands-of-members consumer diagnostics business (160+ biomarkers twice yearly, plus imaging and multi-cancer screening) built on arbitraging a massively opaque lab-pricing system and on population-level biomarker data (e.g., 65% high insulin, 54% high ApoB) that most doctors never test, while arguing AI decision-support (with a doctor kept in the loop) and nutritional/metabolic interventions can outperform the current disease-insurance-based healthcare system, including for mental health.

themes.theme: Function Health's Business Model and Scale

insights.claim: Function Health, launched three years ago, has grown to hundreds of thousands of paying members (reaching millions through broader efforts) and has processed over 100 million individual biomarker data points, generating a large proprietary population-health dataset in a short time.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: A three-year-old consumer diagnostics company amassing 100M+ biomarkers and hundreds of thousands of members signals real product-market fit for self-directed/preventive healthcare and a defensible data moat versus new entrants.

insights.claim: Function Health's core membership is priced at $365/year (about $1/day) and includes two panels per year of over 160 biomarkers, deliberately undercutting the retail price of comparable independent lab testing, which Hyman says runs around $15,000.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: A roughly 40x price gap between Function's bundled membership and retail-priced equivalent labs is the core wedge of the business; any competitor entering this space needs to match or beat this pricing arbitrage.
insights.quote: the retail price on these is like $15,000. It's really inaccessible.

insights.claim: Function Health operates capital-light by partnering with Quest for blood draws across 2,000+ existing draw stations (plus at-home draw options) rather than building or owning its own lab network, and separately acquired imaging company Ezra to add whole-body MRI scanning to its product stack.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: The playbook of partnering with incumbent lab/imaging infrastructure rather than owning it is a capital-efficient model other diagnostics-aggregator startups could replicate.

insights.claim: Full-body MRI imaging pricing has collapsed rapidly due to AI-assisted scan compression — Function's FDA-approved technology now delivers a 22-minute full-body scan for $199, down from roughly $3,000 for comparable full-body imaging services just three to four years ago.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: A ~15x price collapse in whole-body imaging within a few years, driven by AI-shortened scan times, suggests imaging-as-a-commodity-diagnostic is becoming viable at consumer mass-market price points, expanding the addressable market for longitudinal screening.
insights.quote: with our technology which has been FDA approved we get 22minute full body scan

insights.claim: Identical lab tests carry wildly different list prices depending on the venue — Hyman cites a vitamin D test costing $300 at a hospital lab (Cleveland Clinic) versus roughly $10 through Quest — illustrating a pricing-transparency failure in U.S. healthcare that consumer diagnostics platforms are exploiting for margin.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: This scale of price dispersion for identical lab tests is the raw material for a consumer-facing arbitrage business model; it also implies hospital-affiliated labs are vulnerable to margin compression as consumer platforms route volume to cheaper testing partners.
insights.quote: in the Cleveland Clinic lab a vitamin D would be $300.

insights.claim: Insulin testing is framed as one of the single most important and cheapest biomarkers for metabolic health (a couple of dollars per test) yet, per Hyman's own inquiry to Quest, fewer than 1% of submitted lab panels include it, because standard medical practice doesn't systematically screen for it despite the obesity/metabolic-disease epidemic.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: A near-costless, high-signal biomarker being almost entirely unused by mainstream medicine is exactly the kind of low-cost, high-value test a diagnostics platform can bundle to differentiate and to generate compelling population-health data for marketing/underwriting.

insights.claim: Function Health's own member population shows striking, likely-underdiagnosed prevalence: 65% with high insulin levels, roughly 54% with elevated ApoB (a lipid marker the American College of Cardiology literature reportedly weighs more heavily than LDL but that most doctors never order), and about 70% with at least one nutritional deficiency by the lab's own reference range.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: These figures function as both a marketing data asset and evidence of a durable market: a middle-class, non-clinically-selected member base showing this much undiagnosed metabolic dysfunction implies a very large TAM for ongoing testing, coaching, and treatment products.
insights.quote: 54% with high APOB, which is a a lipid biomarker that that most doctors don't check that that is more important than LDL or any other cholesterol biomarker

themes.theme: AI Is Already Outperforming Doctors on Some Dimensions

insights.claim: A cited Harvard study found large language models performed as accurate or more accurate than doctors in comparable diagnostic situations, and patients rated the LLM's bedside manner/communication style as better than physicians' in the same comparisons.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: If LLM diagnostic accuracy plus patient-preferred communication both beat physicians in controlled comparisons, AI-first or AI-assisted triage/primary-care products have a credible near-term wedge into a historically physician-gatekept market.
insights.quote: the chat GPTs and the large language models basically were as accurate or more accurate than doctors in comparable situations

insights.claim: Hyman's own multi-year experience testing AI medical guidance is that output quality has gone from 'terrible to actually pretty good' but is not yet reliable enough to be unleashed on patients without human guardrails.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: The current state of medical AI is 'trust but verify' rather than autonomous — investors should expect continued demand for human-in-the-loop verification layers on top of medical LLMs rather than fully autonomous AI diagnosis products in the near term.
insights.quote: it's gone from terrible to actually pretty good. I don't think we're quite there to unleash it without any guard rails.

insights.claim: Function Health deliberately keeps a licensed doctor reviewing every AI-generated output as a guardrail/compliance layer, and Hyman separately name-checks Open Evidence (a clinical decision-support AI physicians use directly) and Micro One (a data-labeling company that has doctors and accountants certify/retrain LLM outputs) as parallel examples of this human-verification-of-AI pattern.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: An emerging infrastructure layer — expert human verification/certification of medical LLM output — is being independently built by multiple companies at once, suggesting it is a durable category (not a one-off feature) worth tracking as investable picks-and-shovels for medical AI.

themes.theme: GLP-1s: Real Tool, Overhyped for Microdosing

insights.claim: GLP-1 drugs carry roughly a 4% serious adverse event rate and about 75% incidence of digestive side effects; Hyman notes that scaled to 100 million users, a 4% serious-event rate would represent about four million affected people.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: At current adoption trajectories, GLP-1 side-effect rates imply a large downstream market for adverse-event management, muscle-preservation supplementation, and monitoring products — a quantifiable risk investors in the GLP-1 ecosystem should model explicitly.
insights.quote: there's about a 4% serious adverse side effect profile with these. Now 4% doesn't sound like a lot, but if you took a 100 million people and put them on it, that's four million people.

insights.claim: Hyman is skeptical of the trend of already-lean, fitness-focused people microdosing GLP-1s, arguing there isn't good long-term data on it and that he personally maintains low body fat without the drugs through diet and exercise; he frames GLP-1s as appropriate mainly for people who are already metabolically unwell, not as a general optimization tool.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: The 'everyone microdoses GLP-1s' consumer narrative may be running ahead of the safety/efficacy data even among clinicians sympathetic to the drug class — a caution flag for consumer telehealth GLP-1 businesses marketing to already-healthy populations.

insights.claim: Unsupervised GLP-1 use without adequate protein intake and strength training risks significant muscle loss, which lowers the body's metabolic 'engine,' so that if the patient regains weight after stopping the drug (which most do), the regained weight comes back disproportionately as fat rather than muscle — a state Hyman calls being 'skinny fat' or 'TOFI' (thin outside, fat inside).
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: This creates a durable, structural market for GLP-1-adjacent products (protein supplementation, resistance-training programs, muscle-mass monitoring) as a required complement rather than an optional add-on to GLP-1 therapy.

themes.theme: Reframing Mental Health as a Metabolic/Nutritional Problem

insights.claim: Hyman argues a large share of psychiatric symptoms (depression, anxiety) are driven by correctable biological deficiencies — citing a patient the same morning with low omega-3s, low vitamin D, low B vitamins (via homocysteine testing), and insulin resistance — rather than being purely primary psychiatric disease requiring lifelong medication.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: If biomarker-correctable causes underlie a meaningful share of diagnosed mental illness, diagnostics-plus-nutrition platforms have a real (if underexploited) opportunity to compete with or complement psychiatric pharmaceuticals as a lower-cost first-line intervention.

insights.claim: Two emerging academic disciplines — nutritional psychiatry (Harvard) and metabolic psychiatry (Stanford) — are building a research base for treating mental illness through nutrition and metabolic intervention rather than psychiatric drugs alone.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: Institutional academic investment in nutritional/metabolic psychiatry signals this is moving from fringe to mainstream research, a leading indicator for eventual clinical-guideline and insurance-coverage change.

insights.claim: A juvenile-detention-center dietary intervention study (replacing processed food with real food) is cited as producing a 97% drop in violent incidents, a 75% drop in use of physical restraints, and a 100% drop in suicides among teenage boys.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: If directionally accurate, this is a strikingly large, low-cost behavioral-health effect size from diet alone — a data point supporting institutional (school, correctional, hospital) food-policy reform as a public-health investment with outsized ROI.
insights.quote: the violent crime went down by 97% in the juvenile detention center. the use of restraints went down 75% and suicide went down 100% in these teenage boys

insights.claim: Hyman frames American psychiatry as having become overly reliant on medicalizing and labeling symptoms (depression, ADHD, OCD) and prescribing drugs for those labels, rather than addressing root biological/lifestyle causes — a critique he says his own clinical practice and Function's data increasingly validate.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: This view — that psychiatric overprescribing is a systemic, addressable market failure rather than simply appropriate treatment of rising disease prevalence — supports investment theses in root-cause/lifestyle-medicine mental-health startups as a distinct category from traditional psychiatric telehealth.

themes.theme: Emerging Diagnostics: Multi-Cancer Screening and Psychedelic Psychiatry

insights.claim: Function Health offers a multi-cancer early detection blood test (branded 'Gallery') that screens for over 50 cancer types with roughly 75% sensitivity and a low false-positive rate, filling a gap since most cancers currently have no dedicated screening test at all (unlike colonoscopy, PSA, mammogram, or Pap tests).
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: Multi-cancer early detection is an emerging diagnostics category with a large addressable gap (most cancer types have zero existing screening options), positioning it as a high-growth adjacent market to core biomarker testing.
insights.quote: it looks at over 50 different cancers. It it's about 75% good at picking up things.

insights.claim: Hyman frames psychiatry as undergoing a 'two-pronged' revolution — nutritional/metabolic psychiatry plus psychedelic psychiatry (psilocybin, MDMA, ibogaine) — with early data described as promising for PTSD and treatment-resistant depression, including anecdotal reports of MRI-visible brain changes after ibogaine treatment for brain trauma.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: Both government (federal) and state-level (Texas) funding are flowing into psychedelic psychiatry research per Hyman, a policy tailwind worth tracking for the therapeutics pipeline even though he explicitly says it is 'not ready for prime time' or mass population use yet.

themes.theme: The Broken Incentives of U.S. Healthcare — and a New Consumer Behavior

insights.claim: One in three Americans skip seeing a doctor for a health issue because they cannot afford it, despite the U.S. having six out of ten people with a chronic illness, 93% showing some metabolic dysfunction, and roughly 75% classified as obese or overweight.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: This combination of high chronic-disease prevalence and high cost-driven care avoidance is the core macro TAM argument for direct-to-consumer, cash-pay preventive health platforms that bypass insurance friction.
insights.quote: One in three Americans are like skipping going to talk to a doctor when they have an issue because they can't afford it.

insights.claim: Hyman argues the U.S. system functions as 'disease insurance,' not health insurance — reimbursement and physician training are structured around treating diagnosed disease, with little support for the kind of broad preventive data-gathering that platforms like Function provide.
insights.speaker: Dr. Mark Hyman
insights.so_what: Because the insurance-reimbursement system structurally does not pay for preventive data-gathering, expect continued growth of cash-pay, membership-model preventive health businesses rather than insurance-integrated ones as the near-term winning business model in this niche.

insights.claim: Hyman describes an observed affluent-consumer behavior shift where people reallocate discretionary luxury spending (e.g., choosing a $1,000 bag instead of a $5,000 one) toward putting several thousand dollars a year into health testing and tracking, treating health spend as competing directly with luxury-goods budgets rather than insurance budgets.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: If this reallocation pattern is real and spreading (as claimed, among friend groups), premium health-diagnostics spend should be modeled as substituting for discretionary luxury consumption, which has implications for both luxury brands and health-tech customer acquisition targeting.
insights.quote: instead of buying a $5,000 bag or watch, I'm going to buy a $1,000 one and I'm going to put three or $4,000 into my health
